Date: 2026-10-24
Baseline: main, 8dde94a7e261f0e05c42dfe334686cfee288086f
Toolchain: go1.27.3 windows/amd64, GOAMD64=v1
CPU: Intel Core i7-3610QM @ 2.30 GHz (AVX, no AVX2)
Builds: go test -c -pgo=off

main.txt: main algorithm, GOEXPERIMENT unset
main-experiment.txt: main algorithm, GOEXPERIMENT=simd
simd.txt: candidate algorithm, GOEXPERIMENT=simd

All builds use the same benchmark_test.go, including the deterministic random
corpus added in this change. Main production sources are otherwise unchanged.
All binaries run from the working repository with the same fixture files.
The existing name mixed-256k is misleading: that corpus actually has 812032 bytes.
The remaining large corpora have 262144 bytes; tiny-text has 3200 bytes.

Benchmark command for each sample:
  <binary> -test.run=^$ -test.bench=^BenchmarkPureGoGzip$ -test.benchtime=2x -test.count=1 -test.cpu=1

Six samples per build, using all six permutations of the three build orders:
  main, main-experiment, simd
  simd, main-experiment, main
  main-experiment, simd, main
  main, simd, main-experiment
  simd, main, main-experiment
  main-experiment, main, simd

DefaultOptions: 15 optimal-parsing iterations, block splitting enabled.
The reported time is the median of six samples (two timed compressions each).
Each sample also has Go's calibration invocation, excluded from the reported time.
No tests, builds, linting, or other benchmark commands run concurrently.
Measurements describe this CPU and these repository fixtures, not all CPUs or inputs.

main-scan.txt and simd-scan.txt contain the focused scan benchmarks:
  <binary> -test.run=^$ -test.bench=^BenchmarkFirstImprovableLength$ -test.benchtime=200ms -test.count=6 -test.cpu=1
These were run sequentially after the end-to-end benchmarks. The 256-entry
no-hit scan has median 177.0 ns on main and 93.475 ns with SIMD (1.89x faster).
Short and early-hit scans can be slower because the SIMD helper has setup and
call overhead. The end-to-end results include that tradeoff.

Validation:
  go test ./...
  GOEXPERIMENT=simd go test ./...
  GOEXPERIMENT=simd GODEBUG=cpu.avx=off go test -count=1 ./...
  go vet ./... (normal and SIMD builds)
  GOEXPERIMENT=simd GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 go test -c
  GOEXPERIMENT=simd GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm go test -c
  SHA-256 output comparison against main for all six benchmark corpora,
    default and fast profiles, plus a generated fixture in all three formats.
  golangci-lint 2.14.0: the same three existing G703 findings on main and candidate
    (upstream benchmark executable discovery and CLI input path handling).

The initial profile on main attributed 43.81% of flat CPU samples to
firstImprovableLength, 18.46% to relaxStatLengths and 2.65% to getMatch.
SIMD relaxation was prototyped and rejected because updating uint16 path
lengths from the comparison mask cost more than the scalar loop on this CPU.
The retained change only vectorizes firstImprovableLength.

Implementation notes for this Go experiment:
  Float64 broadcast and IfElse use AVX2 instructions in Go 1.27.3.
  The implementation uses AVX loads from repeated scalars instead.
  ClearAVXUpperBits must precede returning to scalar Go.
  An overlapping vector handles the tail so the compiler need not spill
    a live scalar threshold with SSE before clearing the upper AVX registers.

Additional machine:
  i7-11800h/ contains the 2026-10-24 repeat on an Intel Core i7-11800H
  with AVX and AVX2, using the same baseline, toolchain, corpora and sampling
  method. See i7-11800h/metadata.txt and the comparison tables in README.md.
  The files in this directory remain the original i7-3610QM measurements.
  The AVX2 follow-up also found that Windows Go 1.27.3 ignores GODEBUG CPU
  feature overrides. The cpu.avx=off command listed above is not evidence of
  scalar fallback coverage on Windows; see i7-11800h/avx2-broadcast/metadata.txt
  for explicit fallback checks using temporary source overrides.
